He previously received an alkylating-agent regimen and later fludarabine-based therapy, but his disease has now relapsed and is progressing despite treatment. patient_vignette: A 14-year-old boy with localized Ewing’s sarcoma of the distal femur completed neoadjuvant chemotherapy and has had a marked radiographic and symptomatic response. Repeat MRI shows substantial shrinkage of the intramedullary and soft-tissue components, while the pre-chemotherapy MRI demonstrated more extensive marrow involvement. The orthopedic oncologist is planning surgery, but because the tumor now abuts a neurovascular bundle and a wide resection would likely require an above-knee amputation, the team is considering definitive local therapy options. The case is reviewed at a multidisciplinary tumor board with the patient and family, who prefer to avoid major functional loss if oncologically safe. The surgeons note that complete resection may not be feasible without unacceptable morbidity, and final local control may depend on radiation rather than resection. The pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI studies are available for comparison.

patient_vignette: A 62-year-old man is diagnosed with stage III squamous cell carcinoma of the oropharynx after biopsy of a persistent throat lesion and CT imaging showing a primary tumor with suspicious cervical nodes. He is referred to a multidisciplinary head and neck cancer clinic where the medical oncologist, radiation oncologist, head and neck surgeon, speech-language pathologist, dietitian, and social worker review his case together. The team discusses definitive treatment planning, swallowing rehabilitation, nutritional support, and survivorship needs. His family physician is informed of the diagnosis and remains responsible for his general medical care and supportive follow-up after cancer treatment. Because the patient is enrolled in a research protocol at another center, his local team plans to transfer primary treatment planning there, while continuing only supportive coordination and symptom management.

patient_vignette: A 34-year-old man had a left radical orchidectomy for a 1.8 cm pure seminoma. Pathology shows invasion into the rete testis, but staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no metastatic disease. He is anxious about relapse and asks whether the rete testis finding means he should receive less frequent follow-up because his risk is low. The oncology team explains that he has stage I seminoma and recommends surveillance after orchidectomy. They also document that management should not be changed on the basis of tumour size or rete testis invasion alone, and that routine follow-up imaging and examinations will be arranged.

He has mild residual peripheral neuropathy from prior cisplatin but remains ambulatory, independent in activities of daily living, and has an ECOG performance status of 1. He is interested in further treatment and asks about options. The team is considering retreatment with the same regimen because of his prior response, and oral topotecan is also being discussed as an alternative despite his recent return of disease only a little over 5 months after therapy.

patient_vignette: A 52-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed left breast invasive ductal carcinoma presents to discuss surgery. Imaging shows a 4.2 cm tumor with biopsy-proven axillary lymph node involvement. The breast surgeon recommends mastectomy, and the patient is interested in immediate reconstruction if feasible. Because she is node-positive and is expected to receive postoperative radiation, the surgical team reviews reconstruction options carefully. On exam, there is no clinical skin or nipple-areolar complex involvement, and she has no history of Paget disease. She has already had diagnostic mammography and breast MRI for staging. A multidisciplinary visit is arranged to coordinate surgical, reconstructive, and radiation planning before finalizing the operative approach.

The team is considering whether to introduce advance care planning because the family has asked for help thinking through future decisions. The parents worry that talking about prognosis will upset their daughter, who has become tearful during prior hospital discussions. The child herself says she wants to know what is happening and wants to spend more time at home if treatment stops helping. The oncology service already uses a standardized ACP pathway with social work, nursing, and physician involvement, and the family has been offered a structured conversation next week. Her disease is still described as platinum-resistant because the recurrence occurred within 6 months of platinum.

patient_vignette: A 42-year-old quality-control technician in a cable-coating plant comes to occupational health after a routine air-monitoring review. The workplace uses acrylamide-based materials, and the hygienist is planning personal exposure sampling for the technician during a 3-hour shift near the mixing area. The technician has no symptoms, but the team wants a method that will accurately capture airborne acrylamide. They initially considered a 37-mm plastic cassette because it is commonly used for other dusts, but the sampling plan is being revised after a review of the acrylamide method. The hygienist also wants to ensure the sample can be analyzed reliably after collection and that losses during transport are minimized. The only change is that the post-collection workflow would place the glass-fiber filter into a polypropylene vial rather than a glass vial because the glass containers are temporarily unavailable.

She is visibly anxious and says parents are “panicking” on social media, asking whether the school cafeteria food was contaminated and whether this could be a deliberate poisoning. The clinic has not yet received confirmed public health information, and local officials are still investigating the source and scope of the illness.

Over the past 6 months, she has had one near-fall while carrying laundry down the stairs and one minor fall in the kitchen, though she was not seriously injured. She has osteoarthritis and hypertension, takes a diuretic and a sedating sleep aid, and says she feels unsteady when getting up at night. Her daughter notes that the hallway is dimly lit and that loose rugs are present near the bedroom and bathroom. She wants to stay active but has become less confident walking outside and has stopped attending her weekly neighborhood walks. On review, her blood pressure is well controlled, she exercises regularly, and she has no history of prior fractures or other chronic disease-related complications.

patient_vignette: A 15-year-old student is brought to a school health planning meeting after the district notices inconsistent food practices across campuses. The middle school is drafting a new nutrition policy because vending machines, classroom celebrations, and fundraisers currently vary by teacher and club. Parents have asked for healthier options, while students want foods that fit cultural preferences and after-school sports schedules. The school nurse reports that some teachers use candy as rewards, and the PTA is considering a fundraiser built around soda and chips. Administrators want a policy that can be rolled out this semester but also updated after feedback from families, staff, and students. The team is looking for a practical plan that supports healthy eating without ignoring local food traditions or the needs of different student groups.
